utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not lose any or waste any time. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. I can follow the proceedings, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You may sit down. And good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and also good morning to members of the Defence team. My name is Jan Wubben, counsel for the Prosecution, together with Ms. Joanne Richardson, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio behind me, our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink, and her -- assisting her, Ms. Djurdja Mirkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic. I appear for Mr. Naser Oric together with Mr. John Jones. With us are our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries before we usher in the witness? Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just three very briefly. The first is that we've received a -- just now a witness list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's emphasised that it's very potential. Obviously, the more potential it is, the less useful it is for our preparation, and I would just ask my learned friends on the Prosecution to alert us as soon as there's any change, and in particular I assume that some members of the team will be here in early January and we'll be here then and so certainly if there are any changes then, we'd appreciate hearing that from them. The second matter is just to remind the Chamber that we are still awaiting an explanation by the Prosecution of whether the Prosecution gave documents to Ratko Nikolic, and if so, which ones, and why. And thirdly, with regard to Your Honour's ruling yesterday, our your oral ruling, I wasn't clear whether that was going to be followed by a written -- it will be followed by a written ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not as regards today's witness. As regards today's witness the matter is decided. It will the written ruling -- if there will be one, because we might as well decide not to resort to a written ruling. We'll deal with the bulk of the motion and the written response that we are expecting from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I wasn't sure whether Your Honour had found that the Prosecution had satisfied you beyond a reasonable doubt that there was no oppression in the statements being given on camera as we maintained under Rule 95. Because that's our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How do you expect us to tell you yes or no, to answer yes or no to your question if we ourselves haven't even seen the video clip and your submission was nothing but speculation? All you said was: It could -- these persons could and could -- because they were maybe in hospital, maybe they were wounded. I tell you, in your country, anyone who is hospitalised or happens to be wounded and makes a statement, does it on the face of it render that statement involuntary, admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it's the first time I've heard it, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I've made no reference to my national system at all and I wouldn't dream of doing that because we're often reminded that we're not in our national system. You have our written motion. We submitted that there are indicia that these statements were not obtained voluntarily. It's then, we say, for the Prosecution to satisfy you beyond a reasonable doubt. If Your Honours are satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make my submission

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. One moment. Because you don't seem to have registered what we said in the very beginning of this trial. We will never at no moment satisfy this curiosity of yours or this claim or demand of yours. That exercise will be done at the very end of the trial. It's only then that we will decide whether those statements, as they appear in the video, were voluntary or not, and the onus of proving that will always remain on the Prosecution. But until that moment, we are not going to tell you - you or the Prosecution - whether we are satisfied, unless it is damn clear, very obviously clear, at a very early stage, that they could never have been voluntary. In that case, yes, we'll step in and stop the running of the video. But until we are satisfied that there is -- we've heard all the evidence, we are not going to cross --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, this Tribunal has its Rules of Procedure and Evidence. It has its own case law. We have a right to apply to have evidence excluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we even have a right of interlocutory appeal. If Your Honours leaves us hanging until the very end of the trial as to what's going to be accepted and what's going to be rejected, we lose interlocutory rights of appeal which we might otherwise have. And that's why I requested a ruling so that we can appeal if we need to, so that we can protect our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, if that's how you see it, then do what you like, proceed in any way you like. If you insist on an written decision following yesterday's oral decision we'll give you one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd be obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So my staff, please, will start working on that and we will hand down a written decision

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The third matter was simply that I know we're all keen to finish with this witness today. I don't think that I would be more than an hour and a half, an hour and 45 minutes. So obviously is the Prosecution is able to conclude by the first break, then we're in good shape. If not, we may run over until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what's the position with the rest of the week.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have one remaining witness to conclude the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And how long do you anticipate that witness to take?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it is -- potentially is a lengthy witness, but we expect that he will -- we don't expect to go past Friday. No doubt Friday morning it should be completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Di Fazio, do you want to respond to the point raised by Mr. Jones in relation to Mr. Nikolic whether you had actually had the papers or documents to Mr. Nikolic or Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, may I address -- my name is Jan Wubben. I will address it on forehand because I requested Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio to prepare this, and he confirmed to me that he will ready to do an oral submission in that regard tomorrow or the day after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: He's preparing that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you. So we'll deal with that tomorrow. Mr. -- let's bring the witness in, please. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Just on the scheduling, it would be nice to know if we can just settle that. What I was going to suggest was that we deal with these housekeeping matters on Friday at the close of -- well, when the witnesses have completed their evidence, if that's convenient for you and for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a problem to us for sure. MR. DI FAZIO: Then we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But -- that's not a problem to the Defence either. MR. DI FAZIO: Fine. I could address the issue that Mr. Jones raised, and also you'll recall that you asked for an estimation of trial length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: In the Prosecution case. Well, we could deal with that then. And also, there's another issue that may arise - I stress may arise - and that is that we may invite the Defence to agree one or two witnesses for January, and we want to put that proposal to them. And that may, in turn, affect the sequence and the listings for January, which is precisely the question that Mr. Jones raised and we can also deal with that on Friday. So may I respectfully suggest that we deal with all of these matters on Friday, if that's convenient to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. If there's no objection, that's how it will be done. Incidentally, I see that you have also listed witnesses for the 27th and 28th of January. We will not be sitting on those days, certainly not on the 28th. On the 27th, I don't know, but I think we will not be sitting either. So let's continue with this witness. And there is also -- I want to make sure that you have taken note. There is another holiday, a UN holiday, but I think that may have been taken into account. I think the 21st of January or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, Your Honour, I can respond to Your Honour's question. In fact, we did take into consideration the 21st is a UN holiday and we did not schedule any witnesses for that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. I thank you. Mr. Zikic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Good morning to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to proceed with your testimony. I'm just reminding you that you are testifying under oath. Please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Ms. Richardson will continue. We hope to finish with you today. How much time do you think you need, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I anticipate approximately an hour and a half, Your Honour, should do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go ahead, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Richardson: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zikic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to continue the line of questioning that we began yesterday. You testified about the village guard and the fact that they were in possession of weapons and that they had some uniforms.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you this morning is regarding mobilisation by the Serb army, and I would ask whether or not you yourself was ever mobilised by the Serb army, and if you could tell us when that occurred.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was towards the end of May. I was manager of the post office, so the commander came over and he told me to close the post office down. I replied: How should I be closing it down without a decision from my organisation? They will fire me. And his answer was: Don't worry about that. We must use this space to receive ammunition or food, whatever comes our way. I accepted the weapons. Food was a little bit inconvenient, because all those people were farmers, you know, and it was very difficult -- it would have been very difficult for anyone to deal with them. This went on until August the same year. My post office was cut off from our contact in Bratunac, and the mail couldn't make it from Bratunac to Fakovici, so I had to go to Serbia every Monday and Friday. I was ferried across the River Drina by boat to Ljubovija and then back to Bratunac to bring the mail up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to stop you here for a moment. Let's just go back to something you just testified to. You mentioned that a commander came to you and told you that you had to close the post office. Do you recall the name of the commander?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavko Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "commander," do you know what his rank was? Was he a member of the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was all local people. I said commander, but that has a different meaning. It was a -- this was a "komandir," which means some sort of superior or other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you said his name was Slavko Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was a person who resided in Fakovici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct. He resided in Fakovici and he owned a cafe there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the weapons that you just referred to, where did the weapons come from?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no access to that sort of information, but I heard that the weapons had come from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, were you required to do with respect to the weapons?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For as long as I was at the warehouse, if anyone came who still had no weapons, my duty was to issue them with weapons. But on the condition that the commander signs a receipt, or rather, a decision, and then based on that decision or certificate, I would issue people with weapons. And I would also give them between 10 and 20 bullets to go with the weapon, plus obtain their signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned a warehouse. Could you tell us what building this warehouse was located in, and was it a warehouse or was it more than one room or area?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would put it differently. This was not in the proper sense of the word a "weapons depot." It was just some sort of a storage space that we had. It was in the boiler room of the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of weapons were you permitted to distribute, and to whom did you give these weapons?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever was sent over by the commander. I had to issue a receipt to each and every one of them. First it was in Dobosari. They were using up 7.62 millimetre ammunition. It's an ancient kind of ammunition you couldn't just go out and use those. It was used for a pistol, so despite that, everyone wanted those to use for their pistols. There were M-48 rifles and semi-automatic rifles too. There were several Kalashnikov rifles. That's for as long as I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to whom did you give these weapons? And were these people from Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of those people were locals. That's where weapons were being distributed. All those people were locals. There was no presence of any regular army there at the time. All commanders who were familiar with these things. So sometimes it was the case that many of these people who came to get weapons didn't even know how to use the weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when in 1992 this occurred, what month?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received those in late May 1992, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for how long did you continue to hand out weapons to people in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every Monday and Friday I had to go to Bratunac for the mail. We were still receiving our pensions and money from the various social funds, but those couldn't go through Bosnia. I never thought that it would be necessary to begin with. So the answer is maybe until the beginning of -- the end of July or the beginning of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And with respect to the person you referred to as the commandant, Slavko Jovanovic, could you tell us something about him. You said that he resided in the village. Could you tell us what he did for a living?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the relevance of this question, Ms. Richardson? Why don't we move to the substance of this witness's testimony?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I can move past that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, I think you should.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Not a problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do anything else or were you asked or assigned to do anything else by Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do anything with respect to food?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said at the beginning, the food and that storage, you know, those people were not a disciplined group of people [as interpreted]. They were more dissolute. So there was no order there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You also mentioned that the post office was cut off. Could you explain a little bit more. When you say "cut off," and who cut it off and where was it cut off from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness said they were not a disciplined army, and the transcript says "disciplined group of people." Therefore, this should be changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zikic, did you hear what Madam Vidovic has just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand. If somebody is bearing arms, do you always have to say that that's an army? If I say that this was an army of defence of the villages of Fakovici and other villages, neighbouring, the local population, then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That doesn't answer my question. My question was a very simple one. When you were answering the question before that Madam Vidovic put to you, did you say those people were not a disciplined group of people or did you say those people were not a disciplined army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I would like to clarify. If they're bearing arms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, first answer my question. Then if you want to clarify, you can clarify. I will give you all the chance. But first answer my question, because I want to know whether you actually said disciplined group of people or disciplined army. Then if you need to clarify, you will have all the time to clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. If they have weapons, then it's an army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're still not answering my question. Before, when you were asked the question by Ms. Richardson, did you say they were not a disciplined group of people or did you say they were not a disciplined army? Which words did you use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And is there any explanation you would like to give us beyond what you have told us, that, namely, people who are armed could be an army or could be described as an army? Would you like to tell us anything else about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It all depends how that can be characterised. An army is something that I consider to be a body that's under the command of superior officers. It has its commanders. This, on the other hand, was just done without any kind of proper appointment. They were just people. It wasn't like it was in the Yugoslav army or something like that. I cannot really make -- I don't really know how to answer this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's enough, Mr. Zikic. Ms. Richardson, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, with respect to my last question, you said that the post office was cut off?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us what you mean by "cut off."

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fakovici are halfway between Bratunac and Skelani. There are Muslim villages along the Drina towards Bratunac and upriver, along the Drina towards Skelani. Which means that the passage along those roads was unsecured, and you had to cross the Drina by boat into Bacevici and Ljubovija and then go into Bratunac from Ljubovija, and then carry the sack with the mail in your hand and the other material to the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I would like to bring your attention now to the day that your village was attacked. Do you remember what day that was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th of October, 1992. It was a Monday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us what you were doing when the attack occurred?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day before I was gathering corn in a field which is near the village. You couldn't do anything else. The sowing was done in the spring, and since everybody was afraid of everybody else, we abandoned those fields and cultivated only the fields around Fakovici. The day before, with my wife and her sister, we were picking the corn, and we didn't finish everything. And for Monday, we still had about three or four hours more work left. So on Monday we went to pick the corn. Since actually we couldn't go into the field to cut the grass, the grass was as high as the corn. When we got there, I could see that there was a kind of indentation as if something was lying down there in the course of the day or the night. I paid attention and I told them, the others, to stop a little bit. And when I looked, the field was just below the forest. So from that place, you could see the road coming from the forest. And I said somebody was lying down here during the night. That was what I thought. We carried on with our work. We were picking the corn. Then the shooting started and my wife said: Well, it could be some of our people who had had too much to drink and they're shooting now. And as we were speaking like that, we looked down along the Drina, and you could see smoke all along the Drina. We could look -- we looked upriver and you could see smoke there as well. So five kilometres upwards and down the river, you could see smoke. We didn't know if villages were burning further along also. Later, when I came back from prison, I found out that it was about 12 kilometres, six kilometres from Fakovici towards Bratunac and also six kilometres from Fakovici towards Skelani that there was burning. So it was upriver and downriver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember the time of day that you heard the shooting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was exactly noon. I looked at my watch. It all happened at the same time, to the minute, on all sides it was exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall the direction, what direction the shooting was coming from?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was heard from all sides. There was a house there which I called the guardhouse. You have that in the statements. So there was a response to the shooting. There was shooting coming from all sides, and initially that's how it seemed. Later, since the resistance wasn't very strong, the shooting quietened down. The villages up there, both along -- up the Drina and down the Drina, in the villages, everybody had some weapons issued to them. So they put up a little bit of resistance. Only those in the village of Radijevici up the Drina. But I never heard that there was any resistance that was given from Fakovici downriver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What happened after you heard the shooting? What did you do, and I believe you said you were in the presence of your wife. What did you do?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We left the cornfields. Right next to the fields there is a path, like this, and you can take that path to go down to the road, which goes from Bratunac to Skelani. As we were crossing the road, there was shooting behind us as well. I guess somebody noticed that. So we ran across the road towards the Drina. There is a weekend house there belonging to Ilija Markovic on the very bank of the Drina River. We knew that there won't be any shooting from the Serbian side, so all three of us crossed to that side. A woman who we caught up with along the way also joined us, because she was picking corn too. So all four of us left towards the Drina. We were there just below that house for about an hour, most probably. I know that I smoked about ten cigarettes in that time. When I looked behind the house, from behind the house, I could see that my house was burning also, and I told the women: Run. Below the bank from the place where we were to the boat, it's about 400 to 500 metres, less than half a kilometre, and there is a rock above the boat and you cannot see that place except from the side of Serbia. At that moment, I walked with them about two to 300 metres towards the rock but then I saw that my house was burning. There is a pigsty with pigs next to the house, and then I also had a barn with a cow and a calf there. Because -- well, when I saw the house burning, I was afraid that it would spread to the other buildings, because they're all linked. It's okay if the house was burning, but that's a dead thing, but I was afraid for the other buildings. And I knew their tactics. They would overrun the village with a powerful force, including soldiers and civilians. They collect everything that's there. They run into the house. They take the valuables. They didn't take the big items like sofas or refrigerators. They took the small, valuable things. They would collect the poultry. When you came to Fakovici the next day afterwards, there wasn't a single chicken to be found there. I don't know how they managed to catch all of these chickens. Once you let them go, it was hard to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me stop you for a moment. You mentioned "they." Who are you referring to when you say "they didn't take the big items"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, I think everybody knows what happened in Bosnia, so this Court and you should also know what happened. It was between Serbs and Muslims. That day, the Muslims attacked the Serbs. It wasn't only the Serbs who were attacking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have a weapon with you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was issued an M-48. But it was back in the house. It wasn't necessary to carry it around. That's how we felt that day. Had we known what would happen, we wouldn't have gone to pick the corn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say you saw your house burning, did you see who set fire to your house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. You couldn't see that. I was below the bank. I didn't know who was setting that on fire. At that moment, you feel very lost. You don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you see who was doing the shooting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. How could I know who was shooting? There was shooting coming from all sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And after you went down -- after you saw your house burning, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said that before. I saw that the house was burning, and this upset me, but it didn't upset me as much as the fact that I knew that there were pigs shut up in the pigsty, as well as the calf and the cow. So I tried to look from the bank, but I couldn't see well. I could see that the house was burning. But there was another house in the way, so I couldn't see whether the barn was also burning. When I walked a little bit in that direction, I saw that they hadn't caught on fire yet. But at that point, they noticed me, and then they came up to me. First there were two of them and then I don't know how many of them there were. You couldn't really tell. They caught me, took me towards my house, they tied me up there. And then probably there will be some other questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you describe -- you said there were about two of them. Could you tell us, when you say "them," could you describe what they were wearing and could you tell us if they had weapons.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did have weapons, but I was too confused and lost in order to be able to describe to you what they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, could you tell if they were in civilian clothing or did they have a uniform on?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in uniforms. That's true. At least those two who came up first. When the rest of them came, there was all kinds of clothes that they were wearing. There were also civilians amongst them who were wearing different clothing. There was a little bit of everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they came up to you, did they say anything to you, or what did they do?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard them when they shouted "stop," so I immediately put my hands up. There was a group already gathering there. They had caught the Chetnik commander, as they put it, but that was not me, and I never wanted to be anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And after they -- what did they -- you said that they tied you -- tied your hands. Could you tell us, describe for us, if you recall, what they tied your hands with, and did they tie your hands in front of you or behind your back?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were tied behind my back by a piece of rope or something. I wasn't able to see what they used to tie my hands with. Perhaps had I been calm and collected, I would have been able to see that, but I was very distraught at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened with your wife and the other woman that you were with?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I told you that I walked with them so that they could cross into Serbia. However, during the day, the boat wasn't operating. The Milo Djuric forester tried to swim across the river. You cannot see a person when they're close to the bank, but once he had swum a little bit away from the bank, they actually shot him in the middle of the river, because they were able to see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So with respect to getting back to when you were tied up, after you were tied up, what did the men do?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately somebody hit me with a rifle butt while I was tied up. I didn't feel the blow. I felt it only when I got to Srebrenica in the morning. Because I started to cough, but I couldn't really cough, because I had a pain on my right side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they hit you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They hit me on the ribs, on my right side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I was tied up, a man started to come up to me. He didn't resemble any of our people. Muslims or my own people. When I say "our people," I mean the Muslims also from my area. They are no different from the Serbs. This man looked a little bit different. He said something, not "Chetnik," but "chelnik" or something; he didn't know how to pronounce that word. However, Zulfo Tursunovic was standing next to me. He was on a horse. And I was lucky that he was there. And he shouted "no." I'm not sure whether he shouted that or somebody else from that group. There were many people there. But there is enough time until Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you recall -- you said that they were wearing uniforms, and referring to the two soldiers. After you were struck in the ribs, was it at that point that the person who you said looked strange to you, looked different, did he come and join you and the two soldiers after that, and at what point did Zulfo Tursunovic come up to you? Just so that we're clear.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was captured, Zulfo and all the soldiers were there. This was a house -- Serbia was over here and they were on the other side of this house. So I cannot tell you whether one of those two soldiers up there hit me or somebody from that group hit me. Then Zulfo shouted "no" and then somebody said: There's plenty of time before we get to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned Zulfo. Could you tell us, had you met -- do you know what his last name is? I'm not sure if you mentioned it before, but could you tell us if you met him before?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know who he was before, before this day, before October 5th?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in prison with a neighbour of mine who had appropriated some money from a shop in Fakovici. So I went to visit him. I saw him once, but I didn't actually meet him. I wasn't introduced to him. I had heard about him before, that he was -- there were stories that he had killed two Muslims in a cafe in Srebrenica. That's what I know about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of Zulfo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you describe him, how he appeared on that day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was -- well, I don't want to say things that I'm not sure about. I think that he was wearing an olive-drab uniform, that he was on a white horse. He was tall. He's a tall man. Perhaps he's 1 metre, 90 tall. And I'm sure it was him, because when the column started moving from Luka upriver towards Srebrenica, somebody said: Look at this old man, Zulfo, who is 70 years old, just like Musa Kesadzija or Milos Obilic. He looks just like those heroes from your time. These are people who are legendary from the Turkish times. Their hero was Musa Kesadzija, and we had heroes, Marko Kraljevic and Milos Obilic. They said: He's 70 and look at the way he looks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Was there anyone else on a horse other than Zulfo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you observe Zulfo say anything else to the soldiers, the other soldiers who were present?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not a bit uncomfortable with the suggestion of soldiers. It was originally a suggestion of my learned friend, two of people were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we can stick to uniforms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection sustained. Yes, Ms. Richardson, please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The individuals that you observed wearing the uniforms, were they civilian or were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That doesn't -- that calls for a judgement on the part of the witness, and I think we'll probably get into a discussion of what's an army, what's a soldier, is it organised. If we stick with what people were wearing, then it's for Your Honours to draw that inference. A soldier implies an army, and this witness isn't in a position to say whether they belong to an army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Richardson, we've had this -- I don't know whether you were present when we had this discussion before, sometime last week.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was. And could I just respond. I think we're at the point now where we can certainly put to the witness and ask the witness if in this witness's opinion if the person was wearing a uniform carrying a weapon if he himself judged him to be a soldier or whether it was a person in civilian clothes or was this a civilian. I think every time we go through these questions about the person wearing the uniform it's redundant, and I think at the end of the day Your Honours are able to judge for yourself whether the description, the characterisation of the person being described is a soldier or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can assure you we will be in that position, Ms. Richardson. In the meantime, I would suggest that you ask the witness to describe what they were wearing, and you may go ahead also with asking him what he considered them to be. But not beyond that. And please refrain from using the word "soldier" until and unless the witness himself decides that they were nothing else but soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you previously testified that Zulfo was on a white horse and he was wearing a uniform. Could you tell us what you considered him to be at that point?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an expert in these matters, but in my opinion, when that happened, whoever was there, I considered them to be a soldier. A civilian is a person who's wearing a civilian uniform and bears no weapons. Anyone who is armed I would consider them to be a soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to Zulfo, did you see him saying anything to the other individuals who were present and wearing uniform -- and wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they started going from Fakovici, they started kicking me around like a football. And he shouted: Stop pretending to be heroes in relation to an old man. You will -- you have enough time to do that to other people. You should be able to do that to other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when he said this, who was he speaking to? Who did he say this to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a whole column. I don't know how long it was. For a long time I was at the head of the column, because we came up to the remains of a killed boar who had stepped on a mine. So they thought that these were minefields and they let me go first. However, somebody from the back shouted: The Chetnik will kill us all and commit suicide and lead us into a minefield. So they didn't trust me anymore and then they took over the lead of the column.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "the column," could you tell us, was this -- who comprised this column? Was it men, and could you tell us what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't -- I didn't even dare to turn around. I know that when we left Fakovici, at Slavko Jovanovic's cafe, whom I mentioned as the commander, as the komandir, we had to make a detour. We had to go above it, because we were afraid to go below it, because they didn't know if there were any people by the Drina who could fire at them. They just didn't know. When we were passing by the cafe, somebody said: Director or manager, would you like a drink? Because the cafe was chock full of people. I don't know what they were eating or drinking there, but in any case, it was full of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And could you tell us how you were taken from Fakovici? Could you describe for us the route that they took?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know those roads. These are village paths. We were going along the river for about three kilometres. Then we crossed some fields using some paths. All of these were just village paths that they were using. In the meantime, somebody gave me a backpack with some bullets, and it was a soldier who placed it on my back in order to free himself of the burden. And I understand that better, that I should carry than he. It's difficult to explain or describe that, because it was a long column. I was quite distraught. But then somebody shouted: How long are we going to be leading this Chetnik? And then somebody would say: Look at that creek. And it was an area where there were a lot of creeks, a lot of gullies. And then another person would say: Up to that creek, and then by that creek we will circumcise him, and then at the next creek we will cut his throat. Then we would pass one creek and the next and nothing like that would happen. When we passed through Poznanovici, I don't remember anymore how long the trip was lasting. I was tired. I didn't really feel anything anymore. There was a truck. It was dirty. I think they used it to transport cattle before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me stop you for a moment. When you say that they referred to the Chetnik and circumcision, who were they referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims used the expression in reference to any male Serb. They would call us Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was -- this comment was meant towards you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time that you were threatened, other than when you were struck with the rifle? Did there come a time that you were struck again or threatened by anyone?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if there were threats, you couldn't tell who the threats were coming from, nor could I remember, because I didn't know anyone in that column. Sometimes someone kicked me from the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And did there come a time that you -- well, let me rephrase the question. Could you tell us what the weather condition was that day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to all this misfortune in the evening it began to rain. I was slightly glad because of this, if I can put it that way, because I was hoping that it would put the fire out in my house. I'm a little shaken now. If we can please pause for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zikic. As I told you last time, whenever you need a break, please draw my attention straight away and we'll have a break. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, do you feel better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It was just for a while I had a pain in my back, and that's why I only asked for two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But we'll give you as much time as you like to rest, whenever you need it. Just let us know. Just let us know. We'll try to make your stay -- okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, we were -- you were testifying to being captured after Fakovici before the break. Could you tell us if you were the only person that was, to your knowledge, that was taken to -- that was captured that day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You'll probably be asking me further questions about those who were killed, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed I will get to that later. With respect to the column that you previously testified about, could you just explain to us for clarification about the column, and if I could have Your Honours' permission to lead the witness just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think provided as with any leading, it doesn't go to contentious matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Go ahead, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And please take into account what has been pointed out by Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your hands were tied and you observed Zulfo Tursunovic on the horse, did there come a time that you met up or the individuals you described being in uniform and Zulfo Tursunovic met up with another group of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were travelling, like I said, along the river, and then turned into the hills. We reached a village that I had never been to, although it was part of the area covered by my post office. I knew the approximate distance because of the waybills that would be forwarded to me. We came to a source of water with three wells. We sat down and drank water. And the man who was the closest to us, who was next to me all the while, he asked me: Are you still alive? I would like to have some water. And the man who was about seven or eight metres from us, he said: They all had flasks, so that he should bring some water for me. And I said: I will not have a Serb soil my flask. It's a derogatory term that he used for Serbs. Vlah. He took the water, however, and my hands were tied. I just opened my mouth and he poured some water into my mouth. That moment, I looked and people were coming from both sides of the slope, down the Drina River from Fakovici, and from the opposite direction, from Fakovici, the opposite slope. And quite many people assembled there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you describe those people and what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I can't describe anything. I was entirely distraught. All I could see was that many people were arriving. But even if my father came, I don't think I could have told him from Adam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just for -- so that it's clear: The people that you said that you came across, are those the same people in the column or are we talking about a different group of people?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- group sat down. We were the first to arrive. We sat down near the well, and as we were drinking and resting, people started arriving down both the slopes, from two opposite directions, from both sides. From that side and from this side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you see if those people were in civilian clothing or in uniforms? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. I know there were many rifles. They kept rifles, and those people too would sit down and place their rifles next to them on the ground. It was a mixed group, both civilians and people in military uniforms, in a manner of speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And could you -- do you recall how many people there were?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Later I found out -- I'm not sure if you'll ask about this later, but Akif told me later at Srebrenica, and I must apologise to the Court, in order to be able to say this in the original version. Had he known the sort of shit that we were, Akif said, he would have taken 12 people along and not two or two and a half thousand to go through so much suffering for those 12 people to do what they did. I still want to know why he said 12 specifically. I was in the army myself. Why didn't he simply say a squad of men?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We will get to your meeting with Akif in a little while. Could you tell us whether the people that you just described to us who were in civilian clothing and in uniform were Muslim or Serb?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was the only Serb among them. I don't think a Serb would attack another Serb under those conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You described -- testified previously that you did receive some water. Were you given any food?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't need any food at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did there come a time that you stopped walking and you were placed in a vehicle or a truck of some kind? Could you tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just I can't remember exactly. It was dark already and I don't know where this was. I was put onto a truck, and I think there were four other men there. And the rest of the soldiers were on their way back to Srebrenica, on foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And before you were placed in the truck, you walked some distance. Could you tell us how long you walked? Was it an hour or two or more?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think about three hours. We kept walking for about three hours. That's in as far as I can trust my own judgement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were tied the entire time?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters didn't get the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I heard him say "da." Do you agree? Could you answer the question again, please. The question that was put to you whether during these three hours you were tied the entire time. Did you answer "da"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer was yes, and if I may add: All the way to the prison gate, I remained tied, to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Zikic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were placed in this truck, who was -- accompanied you or who was with you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't know a single man there. But I was not mistreated on that truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many men were with you, and could you tell us if they were wearing uniforms or were they in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those four men who were in the truck were wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall what time you arrived in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can answer that. It was night-time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And where were you taken once you arrived in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understand your question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you -- there came a time that you -- that the truck stopped in Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Outside the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And once you were removed from the truck, where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the truck pulled over and there's a road passing in front of the prison. There was something -- there was a source of light from behind. I'm not sure if it was a candle or a light-bulb, and they untied my hands and they said: Why didn't you complain? Your hands are all black. There's no circulation in your hands. And I was left speechless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that -- you testified that -- all right. After -- I'll rephrase the question. After they untied your hands, where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Straight away, they took me into the prison. They banged me against a door. I fell on my stomach and I hit some people's shoes, the people who were standing there. But I banged against their shoes. Yet no one was moving, so I -- the idea that I had was that I was in a morgue, that those people were dead. But then they moved and then I started shaking shoe by shoe, and one of them kicked me with a shoe in order probably to show me that he was still alive. And then everything fell silent. No noise could be heard. And I asked: Is anyone alive here? But you were not allowed to speak a single word there. So I was admonished by one of those people. They said: Just stay silent. There are four of us here who are still alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after this occurred, what did you do after that, after this person --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I heard the witness say there are four of us who are still alive. There are four of us who are alive, and what I see on the transcript is there are four of us who are still alive. Can we have a clarification, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what was said. I didn't exactly phrase it like that, but the exact -- the exact thing would be: There are four of us who are still alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anything else said by anyone?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one was allowed to say anything. At daybreak, I only asked: Are they beating people? And one of them answered: Not only are they beating people; they are using rusty tongs to extract teeth. And then a log of firewood was used to kill someone. I'm not sure I remember the last name correctly, but I think it was Kukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you previously testified about how many people, once daybreak came. Could you tell us how many people were in this room with you, and if you recall the names of these individuals.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found four persons there. One was called Veselin Sarac. Another man was called Radic, Nedeljko. The third man's name was Zoran Brankovic. And the fourth man's name was Nevenko, from Indjija, but I can't remember his last name, or perhaps he never even told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Were you able to observe their physical condition?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the day, this Nevenko was all covered in blood and he never stood up from the corner in which he was sitting, nor did he lie down. He just placed his hands on his knees and he sat there like that. And the other men were also covered in blood and exhausted. I can't be sure about that. That's how it looked to me. I must speak about these things here, but these are stories that I find very difficult to cope with, and these are difficult statements. But those people looked more like dead people than people who were still alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, prior to being placed in the cell with them, had you met any of the four prior?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'd never met any of them in my life. If you allow: Zoran Brankovic, his nickname was Smederevac as I understand, there is a bauxite mine there, and this person called Nevenko, they took part in a competition. They saw an ad in the paper, the Politika paper, and they came to work as guards at the bauxite mine, and their salary was 300 Deutschmark, German marks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did either of the four men tell you how it was that they came to be in the condition they were in that you just described, with blood, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked them whether they had been beaten, and their answer was that they weren't only beating people but that they were using rusty tongs to extract people's teeth and that a man named Kukic who had been brought in with them, I didn't find him there, because that was before I arrived, was killed using a log. There was a stove there with firewood next to it. I didn't see that stove, or maybe I did, but I didn't notice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And when you say "they," when you say the four men, or you were told by the other persons in the room with you that "they had been beaten," who are "they" referring to? Did they say who had done this to them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know whose hands they were in. Who else could have done it? Maybe one of them recognised someone. But I never recognised any of those who were doing the beating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if at this point my learned friend could actually ask non-leading questions such as what -- did they say anything to you or when my learned friend starts with did they tell you, I feel a leading question coming on. We're in sensitive terrain here, and I'd prefer if my learned friend could lead as little as possible; in fact, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. I don't think that the witness is leading as much as you're suggesting, but we'll keep a watchful eye. Thank you. Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe, once it was daylight, could you describe the cell or the room you were being held in with these other four men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we want to know, how big it was, whether it had any windows.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm able to give you my estimate, three metres by two and a half metres. There are bars on the way in. There's a small corridor. You first enter the corridor and then from the corridor you enter the cell. There was a floor, and higher up, I'm a small man, for example, and I wanted to look out and see which prison it was, because I'm familiar with Srebrenica. But the window was too high up for me to reach, the distance between the floor and the window. And the ceiling was perhaps two and a half metres high. I'm no expert in these matters, and I don't think my judgement should be taken at face value. And I wasn't really interested in judging these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were there any chairs or beds or mattresses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was nothing in that room, no blankets, no covers, no chairs, nothing at all. It was totally empty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is back to you, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given any -- where did you sleep?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sleep -- you just mentioned -- you just testified that there were no beds or mattresses. Did you sleep on the floor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Where else? We would lean against the wall. It would have been a bit inconvenient for me to lie on the floor, because I'd had a rib broken. So I tried to lean against the wall the whole time, and that's how I spent both my days and my nights. I don't mean upright against the wall; I would just be -- remain in a sitting position and I would lean my back against the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the floor concrete or another type material?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be certain. It was a floor. I'm so distraught in that prison. I think it was a floor, meaning made of wood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it cold in the room?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srebrenica has a relatively cold climate and I was captured in a cornfield. I only had my trousers on and my underwear, and my undershirt. It was cold, and my jaw was chattering. I'm not sure if it was chattering because I was cold or because I was scared. You are there left without any help at all, totally helpless, and you're drained of any will to do anything in a situation like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you fed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The food was brought in: Cold tea, mostly beans, with a small piece of bread. However, I personally did not take any food. At first I didn't feel like eating. And then secondly, I saw that in one piece of bread, there was something shining. I don't want to accuse anyone, but I thought that it could have been ground glass. This is what it seemed like to me. Please don't take this too seriously. I didn't feel the need to eat. I didn't feel the need to go to the toilet. During the time that I was there, I didn't need to go to the toilet, not a single day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given water?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe it or not, but I don't remember anything about water. They probably did give us water. I concluded, and this will probably turn out to be true later when we went to be exchanged, we were told to wash our faces, and they were pouring water from some kind of a plastic bottle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times a day were you given food?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the conditions you just described to us, that it was cold in the room and you were -- there was no beds, sleeping against -- leaning with your back against the wall, were these pretty much the conditions that continued to exist the entire time that you were held in this cell?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the first day to the last day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zikic, could you tell us about who, if anyone, guarded this cell. Was the cell guarded?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the cell had guards who were supposed to take care of the prisoners. However, I can say freely that the guards were there, but it's as if they didn't exist at all. Because anyone who wanted to beat you could enter the room, which means that they were there, but it's as if they weren't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many guards were there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That changed. We couldn't know what was going on in the corridor. Only the things we saw were something that we know about. There were always soldiers in the corridor. What's more, you couldn't really decipher who was the guard amongst them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "anyone who wanted" -- you just testified "anyone could enter the room," could you tell us about that. Did other people come to the room other than the guards, and what did these people do to yourself and the other prisoners, if anything?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say only this: There was Omerovic Sabahudin, and when he was on guard, he would come to the door, and then he would ask: Does anybody want to go to the toilet? Is anyone thirsty? And during the time when he was a guard, nobody could enter the prison to beat us. It usually happened during the night, when you don't know. We would just cover our eyes so that they would not gouge them out. But as for the rest, they could hit whatever they want. We didn't know who would come in at night, except you could hear Beli said aloud when he appeared in the corridor. And then in the prison, I told you that my nickname is Drago. That's what they called me. They would say: Drago, now you're finished. As soon as you could hear him enter the corridor, the guard would give him the keys and he would ask these four cellmates of mine: How is this Chetnik commander obeying you? They would shrug their shoulders. What could they answer to that? Then he would say: Who of those people, my cellmates, would start to beat me first? They would hit me, but they were weak blows, because they were exhausted. And why would a Serb beat another Serb, especially an elderly man like me? I can't think of how to say that properly. It's about the way I looked. And then he would say: Hit him harder. And then I would start to cry. Hit him harder. Because it's up to the other person to beat me. Because if they don't beat me, they would get beaten. So it's better for them to beat me than to get beaten. I would just ask myself why this Beli hated me the most in this group. And then I would think to myself, when they carried out the attack against Fakovici, perhaps he had some close relatives, a brother or someone. He's a young man. I don't think he was old enough to have a son of fighting age. To this very day, it's not clear to me why he picked on me so much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, were you the oldest among the five prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The oldest by far. I can't remember. Sarac was right after me, Veselin, perhaps he was also another -- younger than I was by ten years. Nedeljko was born in 1951. There were two of them. This Brankovic person from Smederevo, Zoran Brankovic, and this other man, Nevenko. They were in their 20s. Both of them were young.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this Beli that you testified about, could you -- do you recall how many times he would come to the cell?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he entered the cell twice. When he would come, he always had a stick with him. It's a stick this thick. He would ask me to approach the bars and to crouch down. Again, only me. He would hit me on the head. After that, I would have knots on my head the size of walnuts. And then they would disappear within 24 hours, I think. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson, this Beli is a name or a nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what they called him. Later, I heard, when he was being discussed, that there's a village called Pale, but I don't know his first or last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this Beli, could you tell us if he wore a uniform or if he was in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Neither did we. Could you answer the question again, Mr. Zikic, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beli wore a uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I know -- you just testified that you were beaten, the guards would let other people into the cell to beat you. Other than Beli, could you tell us how many other people came in to the cell to beat you, and also tell us if they beat the other prisoners as well.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they beat the others. They would enter the cell whenever they wanted to. They would take out people individually, out of the cell, to some other room. Unfortunately, I was the last one to arrive to the prison, so they would take us out one by one in a certain order. It was worse for me to listen to their wailing and to know what awaited me. I preferred to be the first and then come what may. That's how it was the first time. On a couple of occasions, they would take all of us to this other big room, and there were about 30 or 40 soldiers there. It's very difficult for me to describe that and to tell you how many there were, because there were so many. Then somebody from that group would shout: Who wants to beat whom? The first time we went out, they didn't each choose each one of us. They took this Branko Smederevac. He was standing in the corner. He had good hair. He was a young man. They grabbed him by the hair and smashed his head or banged his head against the wall. At one point he just slid down the wall. He fell. They picked him up by his feet and arms and took him back to the cell. Then they began to beat all three of us. Somebody hit me from the back. I don't know who it was. And I fell down. But he fell down too. I think that he was drunk. Why would he fall down if he's hitting me? I don't know what he used to hit me with. I know that I just fell on my chest at that point. All the others had lost consciousness. They could not walk back. But they had to be taken back to the cell. However, I did not lose consciousness. Somebody perhaps was a little more compassionate and did not want to finish me off. Perhaps they took into account the fact that I was an elderly man, that I was exhausted. But in any case, I did not faint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they use to beat you and the other soldiers with?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the occasion. Usually -- well, on one occasion, one of them told me: Do you know how to dance the Serbian Moravac? If you don't know, gentlemen, that is a very fast Serbian dance. And I said that when I was younger, I knew how to dance it, but I don't know anymore at this age. Do you want me to show you, then? Lie down. And then I was going to lie down on my stomach. However, he said: No. Turn over. Lie down on your back. And he climbed on top of me and danced. I had pain on the left side, and these others said: It's probably your bladder that's been injured, because I felt that pain in that area. I had pains as a result of that. And because of that, I probably got a hernia, which I still have to this day. It's a hernia the size of an apple, and I'm still suffering pain because of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I notice in the record that my question to the witness about whether he was beaten and what did they use to beat you and the other soldiers, but I meant to say prisoners, but I think the witness understood. I just wanted to correct that for the record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- also could you tell us if they used anything else, any other instruments or did they hit you with their fists, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fists, shoes, for example, they knocked my teeth out with a rifle butt. They knocked my teeth out when they tied me back the first time. He was holding a rifle on both of his shoulders, not the way it's usually done. And he had his arms like that over. Then he turned towards me. I don't know whether he just took the gun by the barrel or just struck me, but I lost my teeth. Actually, most of them were broken. They didn't fall out completely. Everybody did as they wanted. There was no rule what they were going to beat you with. We're not talking about a police officer who would use a truncheon and nothing else. They did whatever they wanted and used whatever object they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how often did the beatings occur to yourself and the other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, only when the guard, Omersa Sabahudin, called Cude was on duty, then we were at ease. Nobody would enter the cell. But it depended on the other guards whether somebody would come into the cell or not. When he was working, nobody else would come in to beat us, which means that the others could have behaved in the same way. They could have prevented people from coming in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also mentioned going to the toilet. Were you also beaten going to the toilet, and the other prisoners as well?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not allowed to go out to the toilet except when Cude was on duty. He would ask us. If you came into the corridor, you would be beaten from all sides and kicked. So we had nature call in the room where we were sleeping. It stank and it was no wonder when they would come into the cell from the corridor that they would say: Oh, my God, don't these Vlahs stink. I don't know if you know that word. This is a derogatory word used for Serbs by Muslims, Vlahs, Vlasi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you or the prisoners receive any medical attention while you were in the prison at any point?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. Nobody ever asked for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the guards or the soldiers that would come in, could you tell us if you were aware of whether or not they had been drinking?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people who came in that state also. Like I said, that person who beat me once, when he hit me, he fell down. I cannot be sure about it, but perhaps the command was close by. There were many soldiers there. You could hear singing all night long. And they wouldn't be singing if they were not drunk. I know that. Why would a normal man be singing in the middle of war? We knew, by the way they behaved, when Mr. Oric would come to the prison. There would be a deathly silence when that happened, meaning that Mr. Oric had come into the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "Oric," are you referring to Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
