utterances.text: Yes, Naser Oric. That's when the beating would stop. While he was there. Probably while he was there, because there were some breaks of several hours that nobody would come in to us, which probably was the period when he was in the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you tell us if during the time that you were in the prison, if you were made to clean the toilet or do anything else with respect to the prison.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not able to do any other work. They didn't want to let us out to either see the sun or the moon. But as far as the toilets, that is something that's a really dark memory in life. It was a room that was right next to the cell. There was no toilet bowl. It just had some sort of hole. And then some people would stuff it on purpose with paper and block it. And I think that there was so much refuse there collecting there. I think if a hundred people had gone to the toilet there, there could not be so much urine collected there. I think it was my turn a couple of times to clean the toilet. However, this was something that we all did. Then from that hole, I mean you had to bend over that hole. You had to pull out all the paper that was clogging the hole. But you couldn't do that standing up. All the others were taller and better built than I was and they made a better job of it. I had to kneel down and lean on one elbow in order to be able to reach with one hand into the hole. I tried that, and he pushed me down with his shoe so that I had to lie down and clean. What else can I tell you? But it's something that everybody did, not only me. Thank God it was only on a couple of occasions. The worst thing was that after that, you were not able to wash your hands. You had to come back to the cell in that state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say he pushed you down with his boot - I'm just paraphrasing here - could you tell us who you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the soldier who took me to do the cleaning, but I don't know who that soldier is. Because I didn't know anyone in Srebrenica. I didn't know anyone. It didn't matter if they were in uniform or in civilian clothes. I didn't know anyone. And also, I was so distraught that I couldn't recognise anybody. So I didn't know anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, thank you. I would next like to ask you about being questioned while you were in the prison. Did there come a time that you were taken to be questioned?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Right away in the morning I was taken for questioning. I think it was a member of the army, Mirzet or Mirsad. I don't know what the need was for soldiers to be present in his office during questioning. Anything you would answer was no good. It didn't matter if you were speaking the truth or anything else. It didn't do you any good. Sometimes the soldiers, and I think that they -- if this man turned to his notebook or something, or if he looked away for a second, they would hit us. They were trying to avoid him noticing it. And then on the way out, when I was at the door, there was the man whom I mentioned earlier, who had knocked my teeth out. He was standing outside Mirzat's door. That's when it happened when I was leaving the interrogation. On another occasion, I went to the first floor, because this was on the ground floor, so this time I went to the first floor, where the questioning was conducted by the police. I found that out later. I didn't know what building I was taken to, because I was brought there during the night. So this other person was quite fair. Oh, yes. When I was entering the room, a soldier escorted me, and he tried to enter the room, and he turned him back from the door and it was only the two of us in the office. And he asked me: Drago, do you know who I am? I said: I apologise, but I don't. It would be better for me if I knew. He did not want to introduce himself, but he did say: But I know you. The interrogation was all right. But he did say: How come you don't know anything? And I said: Well, you know, until -- up until the 5th of October, when everything started, I didn't go anywhere from Fakovici. First I worked at the post office. At the time, I was 57 years old. I didn't have any military commitments or obligations, at least in Bosnia. I don't know what the requirements were in the other parts of the country, but up until the age of 55, I had to -- I had some commitments vis-a-vis the army. But at that time, I was 57 years old, so I was no longer obliged to respond.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he -- did Mirzet tell you his name? How did you learn his name?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vojislav Sarac worked in the bauxite mine, which I mentioned before, and he had an apartment in Srebrenica. But he didn't live there. His daughter lived there. So he knew him, and they also knew him. The guards knew him. And I remember one time: He was smoking. He was making his own cigarettes from tobacco. So he asked this guard to give him a cigarette. He gave him a cigarette and he smoked that half. I'm a smoker also. Unfortunately, I have been smoking two packs a day for 40 years now. That's 40 cigarettes a day. To this day, I'm constantly smoking cigarettes. But you can take my word for it that I never even -- the thought of a cigarette never even crossed my mind. It was as if I had never, ever smoked a cigarette in my life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this Mirzet, while he interrogated you, did he hit you or beat you at any point?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not during the interrogation, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he do it at any other point? Did he hit you or beat you at any other point other than outside of the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One evening - I don't know if he was angry or something, but they took all of us to this bigger room - he rushed past several soldiers and kicked me in the stomach with his foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the times that you met or observed Mirzet, was he in civilian clothing or military uniform? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think that he did not have a military uniform. If you allow me to say that in the state that I was in, it was very difficult to notice anything. It was very hard to be aware of details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time that you were interrogated -- I'll rephrase it. Let's go back to when you were interrogated by the police. Do you remember who that was, who that individual was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that person, but he appeared to know me. However, I found out later that this was the former police commander. If that was true. But I tried to live by that Chinese proverb which says: A hundred times heard is once seen. Therefore, I can't state something that I'm not certain about. I do not want to accuse anyone who may not be guilty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the times that you were beaten, did anyone intervene, meaning any of the soldiers who were present, or the guards, to stop the individuals from beating you and the other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said, when they untied my hands, there was this man who asked me why I hadn't requested to have my hands untied earlier, and the other man said: Are you sorry about this, Chetnik? That's the only thing I felt because this man was actually sorry that my hands had turned black because of the bonds. That was the only time I felt anything like that throughout my time in prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after being questioned by the police, were you questioned again any time that you were -- during the time that you were imprisoned in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall the day of the exchange? Were you questioned then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can call that the third questioning, we set out in the morning. We were ordered to wash up, and then we were in the boiler room. They poured some water from a plastic bottle. We tried to wash up. We got onto the vehicle and we spent several minutes travelling. But then the truck turned round and drove back, and lo and behold, we were outside the prison again. So I was told to get off. I was the first to be told to get off. And I was particularly scared at this point. Those four persons had been captured together, but their command was back in Milici and it had nothing to do with us. So they tried, and they drove one prisoner over to be interviewed, to give ten tonnes of flour. I'm not sure if individually or a total for all four persons, ten tonnes of flour. No agreement was reached, but I thought to myself: Okay. Now that we've set out, an agreement must have been reached. They were taking us to be exchanged. But as for myself, my family were not looking for me. No one was looking for me. I was asked maybe two or three questions, the same questions as before, more or less. The soldier who climbed onto the truck with me, and then they would get off one by one. Brankovic was detained a little longer. Those people were returning one by one, but Brankovic was the last to stay behind. And when he wanted to climb onto the truck, there were about ten persons, soldiers, there around the truck. They lifted him up by his arms and legs, four or five of them, and they put a block of concrete on his back, smashed him on the concrete, and he was all covered in blood. And there was foam coming out of his mouth. And someone cried: I have to apologise to the Court again. He said: Fuck your bloody Chetnik mother. If you die right here, you won't be exchanged, I guess. And then he opened his eyes. I wanted to put him in an upright position so that he wouldn't suffocate, but he was -- he weighed twice my weight. And whichever way I tried to pull him, he just would slide back and slipped from my hands. So I tried to do the best I could to put him in an upright position so he could breathe properly and so he wouldn't suffocate. So he made it eventually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Before I leave the topic of -- I'd just like to in fact go back for a moment. You said you were made to clean the toilet. Do you recall also having to perform some type of task with respect to a dog during the time you were in prison?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, it happened to me, or maybe it was on purpose. I was the weakest among them. They told me to come out, so I came out. They were loading some garbage from the prison onto a truck. That truck had run over a dog, and they had spades and everything. They could have buried it or thrown it wherever they wanted to. However, they ordered me to pick it up, and you can see that in the certificate that I showed you. When in trouble, your strength is renewed. I didn't realise what was happening, but I saw a piece of cardboard lying right there. In order to avoid touching the dog with my hands. But then he stepped on my hand and I used my hands to lift the carcass. I put it into the cab and I went back to the prison with my hands like that. I went back to the cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now I would just like to ask you a series of questions with respect to the individuals you encountered while you were in prison. You mentioned Naser Oric's presence. Could you tell us when you first -- when was the first time you met Naser Oric, and where was this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of Naser Oric before I was ever captured. I never set eyes on him, or he on me, for that matter, probably. I can't remember specifically. I think it was the second or the third day he came to the prison and asked me, because I was from Fakovici, he asked me if I knew Urazi [phoen] Jovanovic, and I said: Of course I do. He's a neighbour of mine. What sort of a man is he? I said, as we Serbs do: He's a man of the old kind. He said he got my people's back up so they beat him. I know why he asked him -- why he asked me that. He was caught in an ambush, and two men named Bozic, Ljubisa and Radosav were killed. The three of them were on their way to their village and this was near Fakovici. So those two had been killed and their bodies were found, but the third man was missing. And they were looking for him. But no one knew that he had been taken to Srebrenica. He was beaten so much, in fact, that he was carted to an exchange, cartwheeled to an exchange, and then he was exchanged in Srebrenica and he was then sent to Belgrade, but he died five or six days later. Mr. Naser probably knew the state he was in when he was dispatched to Belgrade. So that's why he asked me about him, about his destiny. Then he asked me if I knew a man called Bozidar Kovacevic. That's from -- he works at my old school. He had for about 20 years. He said: Do you know what became of him? I said: I don't know. He said: He hanged himself by a door handle. He didn't say if it was a door handle or that of a window, in fact. And that's where our first conversation finished. The next time, and I was told in prison that he came once again. He took a hanger out, a piece of wire --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'll just stop you for one moment here before we get to the next time you saw him. Now, you said -- you mentioned Mr. Naser. Are you talking about Naser Oric whenever you say "Mr. Naser"? So that the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. Naser Oric. Who else could it be? First and last name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you tell us how you knew that you were talking to Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he told us, that he was Naser Oric. Those who had come earlier, he would visit them, and they said that he had brought them meat before I even arrived. He would give them pieces of meat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what he was -- what Naser Oric was wearing the first time that you spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a camouflage uniform. When I say "I think," that means I cannot guarantee. I saw -- and I'm telling you that he was slicing up meat and he gave it to us. But I can't be certain about this. I do not wish to say something that I'm not 100 per cent certain about, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed. We don't want that either here before the Tribunal. Could you tell us -- you said you weren't sure it was a camouflage uniform, but was it in fact a uniform?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it had to be something, but I can't tell you what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did there come a time that you met with -- that you were visited again by Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He visited again. He came about four times. If I count all the conversations. Perhaps I will remember the last conversation and then maybe I can remember the second-to-last. He came with a pistol to that hall or corridor and he asked me personally: Do you know whose pistol this is? And I said: Mr. Naser, you're the one holding it. It must be yours. And he said: Well, yes, right now it is, but do you think who it belonged to yesterday? And I said: Well, you know there's no way for me to know this. I've been in prison for some time. How should I know who the pistol belongs to? And he said: Have you ever heard of Arkan? And I said: Yes. And he said: What do you know about him? And I said: Well, I know he's rich, he's married to a popular singer called Ceca. Something along these lines. There was no way I could have known anything more than that at the time. And he said: This is his pistol. Zvornik fell yesterday and it had been in Serbian hands, he said, but Zvornik fell yesterday, and this is a pistol that I used to kill Arkan. I said: War is war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And just going back to the first time that you met -- that Naser Oric came to visit you in the cell: Did he appear to know who you were?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But he probably learned from someone that I was from Fakovici, that I was a manager, because in Srebrenica at that time, there were refugees from my area. So when talking to those people, he probably learned something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember meeting -- or Naser Oric visiting the cell again and that you were given anything by him, you and the other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never gave me anything, or anyone else, for as long as I was in that prison. I will try to remember the third visit he made. He came and he asked us: Why are you all covered in blood? I couldn't exactly look at myself to see if I was covered in blood, but I could see the others. And then he came from that side, for example, and I was facing the other way. I was only wearing a shirt. And I was wiping blood away from my nose, because it was dripping the whole time, fresh blood. I was wiping it off. And he said: Why are you bleeding? As soon as I looked at him, I realised that he did not find this pleasant. And once he had left, I told my cellmates: I think it is over with the beatings now. However, I can't say whether he knew about this or not. They started beating us again the same evening, after he had been to see us that day, asking us why we were bleeding. But I didn't have the courage to ask him anything. Otherwise, I would have said: Well, you can ask the guards, because he's the one who holds the keys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back for a moment to the question that you were asked by Naser Oric about why you were bleeding. What did you tell him in response?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you're asked something like that, you just shrug your shoulders. You can't trust anyone. If you dare to speak up, maybe there will be another beating sooner than planned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were the other prisoners in the same condition? Were they also in blood?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. From day one, you keep bleeding and you can't wash up. If you remain like that -- of course, you remain covered in blood if you're not given a chance to wash up. I didn't wash my face or my hands, not a single time while I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not tell Naser Oric who had beaten you because you were afraid that you would be beaten again?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I object to that question and that's an inference on my learned friend's part. He said he didn't tell the person who purports to be Naser Oric she should be saying who had beaten him and the inference may be -- she may wish to draw that inference but that's not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Objection sustained. And in any case he's already answered the question, Madam Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the other times that Naser Oric visited, were you and the other prisoners in the same condition?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the day. Our condition deteriorated to the very last day. It was difficult for us to say how we looked on a certain day because the beatings continued. So you look worse and worse by the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when Naser Oric visited, your physical conditions were such that it was obvious that you had been beaten?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. It was obvious. You change if you don't eat regularly, for example, and I wasn't eating at all. My ribs had been smashed. I had been beaten. So it was obvious. It was easy to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And other than the one time that he asked why you were bloody, did he ever ask you or the other prisoners again why you were in that condition?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've answered that question. He asked us: Why are you bleeding? And then we shrugged our shoulders, and he saw that my blood was fresh. And he addressed me especially to ask why I was bleeding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving on to another individual that visited the prison while you were there. You mentioned Akif before. Could you tell us when did Akif first visit you at the prison, and also tell us whether or not you knew him from before.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had met Akif before, because he used to come to my area earlier. He came to the prison frequently, but he didn't come in and beat or mistreat or insult anyone, except for one conversation that he had with me. We talked about something through the bars, and he said, if I may be allowed to quote: Did God tell you this or did Allah tell you this? It's all the same thing. You say God and I say Allah, but God is only one. However, you twisted things around. How should I put it? When Dzedo ^- I can't remember what the title was - back in the Turkish times, he would take a pipe, fill it with tobacco. The type was about half a metre long. He would place a 14-year-old Serbian girl on his lap until he was finished smoking the pipe, and the girl was going about her business. This took some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the time that you spoke with Akif, was he wearing a uniform or was he in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Akif was wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the time that he visited, the physical condition that you just described, testified about, being bloody and the other prisoners being bloody as well, were you in a similar condition when he was present?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. But he didn't appear to be interested. It was reported in the Belgrade press later on, in the Borba newspaper. I think there was a heading taken from our conversation, saying "Akif believed in the same blood."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you learn who Akif was with respect to his position, being in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew something, but I found out when I was out of prison he was a komandir. They asked if Akif had been visiting, what it was like with him, whether he mistreated us. My assumption that he was up there and that he said some things because he said: Had I known what sort, well, I'm not repeating this. I think you get the point. I would not have -- I would not have taken 2.000 or 2.500 people. I only would have taken 12 people. That means he was an important person over there because he said: Had I not taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you later learn or know at the time Akif's last name?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Last name, no. I didn't know his last name. He used to come to my area. He did field work there. But when I came to the prison, as he was wearing a uniform and I was totally distraught, he asked me: Do you know me? And I said: No. And he said: Well, I'm Akif. Well, okay. I'm starting to remember now at this point. He said: I'm Akif. And the whole situation looks different, and I remembered the name, and I knew it was Akif. And when I first laid eyes on him, I didn't realise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have a weapon with him at the time that he visited?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He never carried a weapon. I don't know why it was that he said, he said: I'm not carrying any rifles, but I like to have a hand-grenade in each of my pockets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I would like to bring you now to the day that you were exchanged. Do you remember what day that was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 16th of October, 1992. We were told that morning that we should go and wash up and that we would be leaving to be exchanged. So we left. We travelled for several minutes and then we returned, and then we continued. And I'm not sure how far from Srebrenica that was, but we went to the barricades. There were tractors there, all trucks. I'm talking about the Srebrenica-Bratunac road. Looking from Srebrenica, on the right-hand side, up there, there are meadows, and further up there, there's a forest. And I thought to myself: Well, now, probably we're going to be facing a firing squad, because they're taking us to the woods. However, there was some sort of a wire on one side, and then we came across a meadow, and there was a house there, and some 15 or 20 persons outside the house, civilians. I overheard a conversation from the cab, the driver talking. He pulled over there. At that time, under those conditions, that would have been a different thing. Maybe it was just one hour that we stayed there, but it seemed years to me. However, people talked, and probably those, because they said the dead for the living and then Akif was killed down there too, Akif Husic. And I'm not certain what they said. Did they say 19, including Akif, or 19 more. Therefore, I didn't know if it was a total of 19 or a total of 20. I have no idea. And then suddenly you could hear another conversation in the cab. The truck started. It passed through the barricades and continued on to Bratunac. I was certain by then we had passed the barricades, we must be on our way to Bratunac. We travelled for some time. We looked at the tractor near Bratunac. This is called Zuti Most, the Yellow Bridge, the place where we were to be exchanged. Both sides were there. The four men were taken off the truck. During my exchange, the exchange, they tried to make me climb down too. Then I said: Well, let me just take my time. I don't want to be lifted off the truck. I wanted to do it myself, and I did. And then they loaded the dead bodies off the tractor and onto a truck. Because we had arrived by truck. And their dead had been brought there on a tractor. They conducted some negotiations, whatever it was that they talked about, probably exchanging records and lists. I have no idea. And then we continued on to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, is your answer complete?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you finished or do you want to say something else?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We arrived at the command. We went to the clinic immediately. They -- we had a check-up. They said that we should wash first and then they would give us the check-up. However, my wife's sister, her husband is a director of the bank. They found out about the exchange. They came. And my children finished high school and university in Serbia. They found out and sent a message.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, if I could just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more do you think you require?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, no more than half an hour. Only because we have the two videotapes and a picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think you might as well forget starting your cross-examination today, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. That seems right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's better for you as well if you don't start it today and you start it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the other hand, I would like to know, having had twice, more than twice as much time allotted for the examination-in-chief, whether you still require just an hour and a half or whether you require more. You will have all the time that you require. I mean, I'm making it very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. And I certainly need to reassess, in light of how much evidence has been given. Two hours is probably more like it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you this because then you need to decide whether you would be able to finish with the next witness by Friday. If you -- because again he's an important witness. He, just like this one is. If you don't think -- we are definitely -- I mean, we've discussed this before, not in relation to the next witness, but we've discussed this before. We're definitely against stopping the testimony of the next witness halfway and then bringing him back on January to continue. So keep that in mind. If you do not think that it is feasible to finish with the next witness by Friday, direct and cross, then make your own arrangements and send him back home.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But with this witness, with the next witness, we are not going to impose any limitations as to time, because they are important witnesses. They are part of the indictment. And therefore, we need to have sufficient time available. All right. Mr. Zikic, we are going to have -- I'm going to have -- suggest a 30-minute instead of a 25-minute break, if that is agreeable. Yes. We'll have a 30-minute break and then you will need to finish in 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, I have the impression from what I have heard that you may have misunderstood what I was saying before we started the break. I wasn't referring to you when I said the witness would have to return in January. You are not going to return in January. We will finish with you for sure tomorrow. I promise you that. And after tomorrow, you will not need to return to The Hague. So please don't worry about it. You have my word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, now Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in addition, finishing tomorrow by this witness means that we had to make an assessment of the time needed for the projected witness after this witness, and there is a significant risk that we'll have to make a break, stop in between his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's not only due to the time needed by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not a significant -- almost certainty that you would have to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And in addition, there came also a health problem. He will visit the doctor this afternoon, and that makes for me, my advice to reschedule him for the beginning of January. That's better. And to address also the household matters on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Or be prepared to address them tomorrow. If we finish with this witness before -- in good time, leaving us sufficient time to address the other matters, we'll address them tomorrow. Why reconvene on Friday when we can finish everything, deal with everything and conclude everything tomorrow? I don't know what's your approach, because this concerns you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We certainly wouldn't have any objection to that course, and it's a matter for the Prosecution whether they want to try and fill Friday morning with perhaps Ms. Manas. I don't know. It's a matter for them. Certainly no objections to housekeeping on Thursday afternoon if we finish on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thursday when we finish with this witness. If we don't, obviously we adjourn until Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There's no question about that. But if we can finish tomorrow, everything, we'll finish everything tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will look also into the matter suggested by the Defence counsel for Ms. Manas but this is kind of all of a sudden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would leave Ms. Manas for January. She is probably already preparing for her Christmas holidays. So I wouldn't try to put in the agenda more than -- anyway, it's up to you. I mean, we'll accommodate you, obviously, as you require, both of you. But be prepared tomorrow to discuss the few housekeeping matters that we have pending. You will need to alert Mr. Di Fazio about that as well, and Ms. Sellers, in case she also has matters to address. And after tomorrow, after we finish with this witness tomorrow, we'll start and hopefully conclude on the other witness. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So now, Ms. Richardson, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I continue with my examination, there has been a matter that's been brought to my attention with respect to the transcript. When Mr. Zikic previously testified to being told a story by Akif, which is -- I'll give you the transcript -- I believe everyone may have a copy of the transcript, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does the Defence have a copy of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. We've just received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Evidently, the translation of his last sentence, at the end of the story, was not translated. And this was brought to my attention, and so just for the record, I think one of two things may need to be done. Either have the witness repeat the story briefly or, if he could remember what the very last line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But can you just tell us what the last line was and we will ask him whether he agrees or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I can suggest -- I can do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I believe the last line was: When the man responded that he was too old and the girl was immature. Now, it could be that in B/C/S that's a different -- it's said a different way, but maybe we could have Mr. Zikic confirm that that's what the last line of the story was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I will do it. Mr. Zikic, when you were giving evidence about this Mr. Akif, you told us at a certain point he told you: Did God tell you this or did Allah tell you this? It's all the same thing. You say God and I say Allah, but God is only one. However, you twisted things around. How should I put it? When Dzedo, I can't remember what the title was, back in the Turkish times, he would take a pipe, fill it with tobacco. The pipe was about half a metre long. He would place a 14-year-old Serbian girl on his lap until he was finished smoking the pipe, and the girl was going about her business. This took some time. Did you in addition to this also say when the man responded that he was too old and the girl was immature, did you say anything along these lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How would you fit it in? In other words, we have this man Dzedo smoking the pipe with this 14-year-old Serbian girl on his lap. And what's the end of the story?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is why you are such a bad bunch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I would leave it at that, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zikic, just getting back to the exchange for one moment. You mentioned that there came a point that the exchange did in fact take place, but could you just briefly tell us, and you may have mentioned this before, but could you just briefly tell us what happened prior to your being exchanged. Did there come a point that you were taken to be exchanged and then returned, and then taken back out again? Could you just clarify for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told in the morning to wash the blood off, that there will be an exchange. We passed through Srebrenica for a few minutes in the direction of Bratunac, but then the truck came back again in front of the building where the prison was, in front of the SUP building. Then they took one by one off the truck. I was the first one. I went to Mirzat, and with a couple of words, he told me to go back to the truck. Then these other two climbed back on and when Smederevac was supposed to climb back onto the truck, four or five people took him, lifted him up off the ground and threw him down on his back on the asphalt. He started bleeding from his nose and his mouth. And when they wanted to throw him back into the truck, they could see that he was foaming at the mouth. Probably afraid that he would die. They told me: Open his mouth. And even though I was not very strong, I managed to open his mouth. He opened his eyes. Then I had to pick him up and make him sit up straight next to the cab of the truck so that he wouldn't suffocate. I don't know what else you would like me to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll move on past this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I would suggest you do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honour, I would like to have the witness -- will be shown a video, Prosecution's Exhibit 446, video number --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have it available?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I believe so. I'd just appreciate some clarification of what scenes precisely are going to be shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm going to ask Ms. Richardson, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, these were the scenes of the place where Mr. Zikic was held and they were shown previously, I believe, with a witness that Mr. Di Fazio --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Okay. All right. In other words, do I take it that you are just going to rely on this video without then referring to photos?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the photo is another matter. I'm not showing any photos for the prison. Just for clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, if you could just take a look at the screen. It's in Sanctions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is where we start?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, can you see the screen and the image in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like me to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot recognise the building, because I was brought in during the night, and I never left the building except when I was talking about picking up that dog, which was right next to the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But are you in a position to recognise it now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Next.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If we can -- the video. It's a clip, so if we can continue playing the video.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I recognise this part. Unless it's footage from some other building, but this part here is the toilet. These are the stairs leading up to the floor, the first floor, where I was interrogated. This is the police building. The corridor. The toilet. I never left the prison or the cell except to go to the toilet, twice, so I cannot know any more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, I think we can just -- I think that will conclude how much we want to show the witness at this point. We can stop the video now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zikic, were you able to recognise from this video the cell that you were being held prisoner in with the other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and no. I couldn't tell you that I'm a hundred per cent sure that I recognised it, but I see that the cell or the room is right next to the toilet, so it could be that. There was only a wall between the cell and the toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, at this time I'd like to have another video shown to the witness, and this is Prosecution's Exhibit 98, video 0002554.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, this is the video, part 1 of the videos that the Defence has objected to and which was the object of the oral decision handed down yesterday by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Stop, stop, stop. Do you need to have -- to run this also with the sound? If it's only for identification purposes?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's not necessary to run it with the sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's oppress the sound for the time being and show own the pictures, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Veselin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name of the person that you can -- do you recognise that person on the video?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Veselin Sarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we could just show a little bit more of the video. If you could just take a look at the video again and tell us if that's the condition that he was in, that you recall that he was in on the day that you were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The footage was made on the same day that we were exchanged when we came to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson -- okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, please take a look at this other person that's being shown to you. Do you recognise this man as one of the other prisoners who was exchanged with you in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nevenko, but I never knew his surname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And thank you, and we can show the clip of the next person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nedeljko Radic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was also exchanged with you in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I would like to add that I was picked up earlier and I was taken to my sister -- to my wife's sister's house, so I will not be in this footage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: We can end the video at this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us if both or three individuals are in the same physical condition as they appeared to you the day you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is there another individual who was exchanged who was not seen by you in the video?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Zoran Brankovic was sent to the hospital straight away. He didn't have any time to wait. They wanted to have him for x-rays. I was picked up and Zoran Brankovic was sent to the hospital, I think in Loznica, right away, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the day you were exchanged, the date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he said it. The day of the week, you mean or the date?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The date. If he said it, it's fine. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he said it already.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you some questions about the injuries you received while you were in prison in Srebrenica. Could you tell us what type of injuries you received from the beatings.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have medical certificates. I had two broken ribs, one possibly fractured, beatings or blows all over the body, in the back, in the front, in the stomach area, and so on. And you can see that from the medical findings that I have. My teeth were knocked out. I don't have that recorded because I never thought that this would be needed. As far as the findings, the medical diagnosis, I have that because I had to go and see a doctor. I had problems with my eyes. They were so bloody and very swollen, and the doctor was asking himself: How was it possible for me to walk around at all with eyes in that condition? So then they gave me immediately some kind of ointment and they put dressings or compresses on my eyes so that they could help me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your hearing affected?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I always forget something. I am having complications because of my hearing. Well, perhaps you wouldn't be interested in that, but when I'm watching TV with my wife, I turn it up very loud, and then she leaves and goes to my brother's to watch television. But had I not had good hearing, I would not have been able to be the manager of the post office and do all of the work there, except for those who actually delivered the mail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And the injuries that you suffered, are any of them -- were any of them permanent? For instance, did you receive an injury to your arm, and is that still a permanent condition?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to explain that to you in the following way: On our way to the exchange from Srebrenica to Bratunac, Beli came along, that person from Pale. I forget his name. He stopped the truck, climbed up on a tyre and hit me with a rifle butt on my right shoulder, saying: Farewell, Chetnik. So this arm I can hold up straight, and this other arm I can only raise as far as this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like the record to reflect that the witness has raised his arm midway, just below his right shoulder, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Richardson. The Trial Chamber has had an opportunity to notice that as well. So it goes on record. Do you have the medical certificates? Are you tendering them?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Your Honour. I can do that at this time. Could I just ask the usher to give that back to us for one moment. I think there's something else attached that shouldn't be there. Your Honours, so as not to waste time, I'll get back to the medical report; we're removing something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, could you tell us if you have any problems with your digestion and are you on medication at the moment?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went to see the doctor yesterday and he prescribed me everything that I needed. Because from the -- during the time that I was in prison, I did not have any food and I did not pass a stool for the period that I was in the prison. 16 days after I was released, my son went to the pharmacy and he brought to me medicaments that I am still using today, and I cannot have regular bowel movements unless I take this medicine, and then, if I don't take the medicine, I get terrible pains in my lower stomach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were your feet swollen and did you lose weight as a result of your imprisonment in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My feet were swollen. Of course, I didn't even show that to the doctor. There was no need to do that. I didn't know that I would need that information sometime. When I was in the prison, I was wearing shoes, my own shoes, in my proper size, but they were constantly wet. The skin on my heels used to be very smooth, but -- and it was very thin skin on my soles. However, when I came to my son's, the soles on my feet had such a thick callus that for some time afterwards I had to wear shoes that were two sizes bigger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you lose weight?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. When I came to Bratunac, I told you that my -- the husband of my wife's sister came to take me to his house. We came in front of the house. I stepped on the stairs. And again, I repeat: They called Drago. He asked me: Drago, please. Stop on the stairs so I can explain something to Nada, my wife, my sister-in-law. I stopped. I didn't hear what he was telling her and she shouted -- his name is Budimir. She said: Budimir, have you gone crazy as well? And I heard the reply. He said clearly: Drago is standing on the stairs. Please stay calm.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have a moment for the witness to compose himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we need -- how much is this going to --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you that we continue, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you need a short break, Mr. Zikic, we can give you a short break. You don't need to worry. You're not going to return here in January. We will finish with you tomorrow for sure. But if you need a short break now, we'll give it to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that even if we put it off for seven days, I would still be affected by it. I will be the same later also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's continue. But if at any time, Mr. Zikic, you would like us to stop, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you hadn't completed your answer. It had to do with your physical appearance.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I will tell you that when I finish what I had begun so it will all fit in. When she opened the door, she stopped and she stared at me with wide-open eyes. She started to hug me. Budimir shouted: No. He is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last of that sentence.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took my hand and it was only just two more steps. My sister-in-law took me straight to the kitchen, Nada. I stank all over. I asked to go to the bathroom. When I got up to go to the bathroom, my sister-in-law brought out the mirror from the bathroom. I went into the bathroom. Budimir gave me a bath. Of course, he gave me some of his clothes and then I went into the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zikic. And my final question to you about your injuries is whether or not you're on medication and are you able to sleep?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am using a medicine called Bescedine [phoen] and it's a tranquillizer which you can also use for sleep. And this is something that the doctor also prescribed to me yesterday. So I trust that doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the reason that you're unable to sleep the result of what you experienced in the Srebrenica prison?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That is a very leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would avoid that question, because he can only tell you what he thinks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. At this time I'd like to tender the medical report. If we can have Prosecution Exhibit. And I'd like this report to be shown to the witness just briefly, for him to identify it. Actually, Ms. Usher, I'd like that particular document, the one that he's looking at at the moment, to be placed on the ELMO. Yes. And if you could not give him that one. Yes, that one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, please take a look at the monitor in front of you. Do you recognise this document? Do you recognise this document, Mr. Zikic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the report that was given to you by the doctor who examined you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I believe -- I'm not sure if it was given a number, Prosecution's exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will be given Prosecution Exhibit P?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, P464.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Siller. There was another document that you --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I apologise. It should not have been attached. I just needed the medical report. So we will collect those at the end of the session. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Registrar -- usher, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zikic, at some point you returned to your house in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us what the condition of your home was.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had burnt down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment, Your Honour. We'd like to have a photograph shown to the witness, and if we could have a Prosecution's exhibit given to this photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Zikic, do you recognise what's in the photograph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I believe it's in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would show him the photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's more practical. If you could just take a look at the hard copy of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness is being shown a photo bearing ERN 01088086.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, do you recognise that photograph and the house in the photograph, I should say

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whose house is this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavoljub Zikic's house, or rather, my house. What you can see towards the top of the photograph is a gable. It has bricks on both sides, so it didn't fall down, but the roof had burned down. And this house next to mine, for example, went like this. And this part of the house is six by four metres. And the continuation on this side is seven by four metres. And that's why, lower down, you can only see this thing up there was knocked down, this continuation here that you can see. So that part of the house was totally destroyed. And this part was left without a roof, but the floor was still there. So the water went away when the house was destroyed, and everything just collapsed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first see your house after October 5th? Do you remember what month it was that you returned to Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. On the 16th of October I was exchanged, on the 16th of October. I spent the evening and the night at my wife's sister's place. The next morning, my son came to pick me up just across the way from Fakovici, across the Drina. He didn't go to Bratunac because his mother would not allow him. She was afraid that the Serb army might seize him or mobilise him, so he was waiting for me in Bacevci and we were waiting to be ferried across and then my wife went to Fakovici. I could no longer cope. So we're talking about the 18th now. So I set out too. May God be my judge, I said at that time, even if I were to fall into their hands again, I just want to go back and see my house. And then they may as well take me again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think at this point maybe we should conclude for today. I think the witness may need at least five minutes. From where I am he seems -- Mr. Zikic -- maybe I should ask him if he needs a few minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, do you need a few minutes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you saw your house, and as you're looking at the picture and the damage that you observe in the picture, is this the damage that you observed on your house on that day when you returned?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same thing, but you can't see the continuation up there because it's gone. There's only one part that remains, down there, but it's maybe half a metre high from that side. From this side, you can't see anything that's up there. It's the angle at which the photograph was taken. You should have a photograph taken from the other side to get the right impression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this damage that you observed to your home, this was -- this damage was done during the attack on Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I do object to that question because the witness has given evidence about what he saw. He saw his house burning. He didn't see anyone set fire to it. That evidence has been given and to revisit is in my submission pointless.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm trying to at least set the record straight that this is not the damage -- that he observed this damage after October 5th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But then put the question. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm trying to get there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just ask the question whether on October 5th this was the condition in which he saw the house, his own house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, on October 5th, was this the condition of your home, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same condition as we see in this photograph. The upper portion -- if the photograph had been taken from a different angle, we would be able to see the other side of the house, because if you look at the hill just behind, there's a continuation of this house. I'm not sure how I should describe this or explain this. I'm not an expert in these matters. I can't be expected to assess the damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think he's answered the question. Mr. Zikic, before the -- before October 5th, was your house in the condition that you see it in this photo or was it intact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, how could it have been damaged before it was even set fire to? I was watching on that day. I watched my house burn, but not only my house. Along the River Drina, along the 12 kilometres, six houses in Fakovici, in both directions along the River Drina, were burning -- for six kilometres, not six houses. Along the Drina, Grabovica, village by village, Vranesevici, Popovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry. Enough. I think you have given us your answer. Next question, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zikic, on the day of the attack, did you observe anyone taking any of your property during the time that you were -- on the day of the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because we had fled. Once I saw the house burning, the houses that were burning earlier were those closer to the creek and then one by one, and then we fled to the river-bank. So what's more, I didn't even see anyone while the house was burning. It was only once I had been captured that I saw soldiers near my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you own livestock and did you see anyone taking your livestock at any point during the attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I owned two fat pigs. It was the month of October and we slaughter these pigs in November. They must have been 200 kilogrammes each. I had about 70 chickens, maybe in about 15 or 20 days they were supposed to be slaughtered. I don't know the exact number of hens that I had. I had a cow and a calf. I said a calf, but it was because of this calf that I was captured in the end. That's what I thought to myself. Well, I was at the river-bank, I saw the house burn and it didn't know how to cry. Because it was nearby, I was afraid that the fire would spread to my livestock. I tried to go back to see if the cowshed and the stable were still in place. They saw me and the whole thing actually happened because of this unfortunate cow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you see anyone taking the cow?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they tied me up, the street and the garden, there was lots. My brother has a huge garage but he still didn't have a door built. There was lots inside too. As I said before, they put themselves up there because it was some sort of a shelter, because they were afraid, since they didn't find anything at the Drina River or from Serbia that there would be no firing. I saw a person from Poznanovici who I used to know and see a lot of earlier, but I don't know his first and last name. There were 1.000 people there. It's hard to point your finger at someone and say who the person is. The cow had been taken out of the shed and the calf I didn't see at all. Maybe they had taken it away earlier, but this was not something that I saw. And I didn't care at the time. There was a lot of noise, and this civilian took the cow away. It was -- the cow was so powerful that it soon got the soldiers tired and the cow must have been scared by the sounds of shooting. What else can I say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And with respect to the houses you saw burning, could you tell us who the owners of those homes that you saw burning, and are these homes in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I could only see the houses burn in Fakovici. There was smoke coming. I didn't see it with my own eyes. I just saw that it was burning. In Fakovici, Djordje Stevanovic's house was the first to burn down. The second house was the church, the church where priests live [as interpreted]. The third house was Drago Jovanovic's cafe.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please may we just clarify this. The witness did not say that the church was burnt but rather, the church building where the priests live, and the transcript says the church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, and it applies also to the Prosecution, please, when you -- when the witness is giving evidence, you have no right to stand up and start talking without our permission. Yes. Let him -- the witness should not be interrupted unless we decide that he should be interrupted, especially since it's a question of interpretation and transcript. Now, Mr. Zikic, you were saying: At that time I could only see the houses burn in Fakovici. There was smoke coming. I didn't see with my own eyes. I just saw that it was burning. In Fakovici, Djordje Stevanovic's house was the first to burn down. The second house was the church, the church where priests live. The third house was Drago Jovanovic's cafe. Let's continue and then we correct that part later. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fourth house belonged to Draga Bozic. The woman died and now her son is Petar. The fifth house is the house belonging to Milos Bozic, the sixth one to Bozo Bozic. And now I'm going back. The seventh house is my house, Slavoljub Zikic. The eighth house belongs to my brother, Bogomir Zikic. Across the way from my house, two, three school buildings which were used for educational purposes. And the next one is the forest-keeper's house, and then the next one, my brother-in-law, Radoj Markovic's house. His brother Radomir Markovic's house. Ognjen Markovic's house, Goran Markovic's house, Andrija Markovic's house. That's it for the time being.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did any of your relatives die in the attack on -- I'm sorry. With respect to the houses you just listed, they're all in Fakovici? So that we're clear.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you lose -- did any of your family members die in the attack on Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB ZIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put together a list. I didn't even know. I thought that I would only testify about the time I spent in prison in Srebrenica. So I put together some information when I was captured. I thought the Tribunal would want to know if anyone was killed, so I put together all this information, first and last name, and the village. If I may be allowed to read this out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be my final question, and if the witness would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Mr. Zikic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long is this list? How many names do you have on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll take probably three or four minutes to read this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll ask him for it later, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: First I was wondering what the list is, if it's something he's prepared himself, for it seems to be in a book firstly. And secondly perhaps he could submit the list rather than read it out. Because it seems to be in a book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where are you reading from? Where are you reading from, Mr. Zikic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Personally, from a monument that is now in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But are you reading from a book or from notes that you have made yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the notes, if you care to have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed with this and then we see it later, Mr. Jones. What difference is it going to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It just saves time if we receive the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've only got ten minutes left and he's going to take three of them, so let's move ahead. Mr. Zikic, could you please read out those names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Attack on Fakovici the 5th of October, 1992. People who were killed. Radoj Markovic, Fakovici; Radomir Markovic, Fakovici; Slavka Markovic, my sister; Olga Markovic; Djoko Jokic, born in 1958; my son-in-law, Svetozar Djokic; Sreten Djokic; Milovan Djokic; Nikolic Petko; Cuba Nikolic; Milovan Nikolic; Miroslav Ivanovic; Vladin Vasic; Stanoje Vasic; Vidoje Djukic; Radovan Djukic; Milutin Ristic; Zarija Ristic; Desanka Bozic; Stojka Stjepanovic, Milomir Subotic; Rade Savic; Milja Despotovic; Petra Prodanovic; Danilo Djuric. That's in relation to the 5th. And those who were killed in an ambush before and after, if you're not interested, I don't have to go through this. What I've read out now is in relation to the 5th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's what we are interested in. Any further questions, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zikic. I do have copies of what Mr. Zikic just read out if the Court as well as the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does it interest the Defence or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, as we all know, Mr. Oric isn't charged with any crimes against the person, so it's probably not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You want to file a list you may file it, but again, at the end of the day, it's not part of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the names have been read out by Mr. Zikic. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can rest for today. Mr. Zikic --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to give a number to this exhibit. This will be 46 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 465, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The photo bearing ERN 01088086 is being marked as Prosecution Exhibit P465. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just to be clear, I understand the Prosecution has concluded their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Because it wasn't said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. It's -- but that's what I understand. Yes. Anything else, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Richardson, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I do have copies of Prosecution's Exhibit P448. I believe it was used yesterday. And I'd just like to provide copies. Thank you. Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Zikic, we will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
